set.hook: Nine tables on Rua do Forno, four guests a table at most, the cataplana the owner tells you to take.
set.why: The house has kept its door open on Rua do Forno for more than fifteen years, and it stays deliberately small: nine tables, none set for more than four. The menu is short and Algarvian, and the dish people come back for is the seafood cataplana, the copper pot brought shut to the table and opened there. Razor-clam rice from the Ria Formosa and plain grilled fish of the day fill out the rest of the order.
set.verdict: The tasca to put first on a Faro list when the guest wants the regional repertoire cooked straight. Ratings vary by platform and a minority of diners mention uneven service, but the cataplana is the constant in every account. It is dinner only on most listings, and the room is too small for a crew table: divide it into fours or go elsewhere.
set.signature: Cataplana de marisco, the one the owner recommends that night
set.caveat: Tables of four maximum; no bookings June-September (first come), so book in the off-season; hours conflict, call ahead

set.hook: Petiscos made from scratch on Rua do Compromisso, in a room of old furniture and odd plates.
set.why: The room looks assembled from a family attic: old furniture, mismatched crockery, kitsch portraits on the walls. The kitchen cooks petiscos, the Portuguese small plates, from scratch and from what the market has, and the list changes often. Reviewers name the pork stew, a fish soup, green beans in tempura batter and prawns, and the vegetarian side of the menu is large enough that vegan diners in Faro single it out.
set.verdict: The right table when guests want to share a dozen small plates rather than commit to one pot. It is inexpensive, the cooking is homemade, and it handles mixed tables of meat-eaters and vegetarians without fuss. The room is small, some find service slow, and it may close for the winter: do not promise it for November without a call.

set.hook: A big adega by the station where Faro families celebrate and the picanha sizzles on its own stone.
set.why: Adega Nova sits near the train station, away from the harbour, in a long room of tiles and brick that fills with local families on celebration nights. The dish Fodor's names is the picanha na pedra: the beef arrives raw beside a hot stone and you cook it yourself, slice by slice. Reviewers also send people for the grilled sardines, the pork stew and fish off the grill.
set.verdict: The value address of central Faro, and the place to feed a large crew without a plan. Expect noise, long shared-style tables and occasional confusion with orders. Bring cash: reviewers say it is cash only and signed as such, though one official listing says cards are accepted. Opening days conflict across listings, so ring before a weekend.

set.name: Mercado Municipal de Faro
set.hook: Faro's covered city market: the day's fish, fruit and greens, and a bifana counter for breakfast.
set.why: The current building on Largo Dr. Francisco Sá Carneiro opened in 2007, and the city still throws it a birthday each February: in 2026 the 19th was marked on 21 February with folk music and a cake. Inside are fish and shellfish stalls, fruit, vegetables and charcuterie, with an underground car park and the citizens' service office in the same building. The breakfast ritual is a bifana at Snack Bar da Xica's counter.
set.verdict: A working market, not a show: smaller and plainer than Olhão's, useful for provisioning in the centre and for a fast breakfast. Go early, when the fish is laid out and the bifana counter is busy. Stall hours vary and no official schedule surfaced, so check the day before you plan a galley run around it.

set.caveat: Mornings are best; official hours not found, stalls keep their own

set.hook: Twin red-brick halls on the Olhão waterfront, voted one of the Novas 7 Maravilhas de Portugal in 2026.
set.why: Two red-brick halls stand on the Olhão waterfront, inaugurated in 1916 for the Algarve's largest fishing port: one for fish, one for fruit and vegetables, with tile panels of the fishing life inside. On 12 September 2026, in a public vote at the final in Sintra, they were elected one of the Novas 7 Maravilhas de Portugal. On Saturdays an outdoor market spills along the front with produce, cheese and cured meat.
set.verdict: The best fish market on this coast and the one to show a chef: lagoon clams, octopus, the morning's sardines, Ria Formosa salt outside. It is a morning place; by eleven it is winding down. The 2026 award will bring more visitors, so arrive early, and on Saturday come before nine for the boats and the outdoor stalls.
set.signature: The Saturday-morning fish hall, then the outdoor stalls
set.caveat: Mornings only; hours unofficial; busiest Saturday

set.hook: A cash counter inside Faro's market griddling garlic-marinated pork bifanas from seven in the morning.
set.why: The counter sits inside the Mercado Municipal, at nos. 10-11 on the square, and opens at seven, when the fish stalls are still setting up. Reviewers describe lawyers, doctors, teachers and fishermen standing side by side for the same thing: thin pork marinated with garlic, griddled and folded into a roll. Faro food tours have started here for years, and the special adds bacon, cheese and a fried egg.
set.verdict: The city's breakfast bifana, and the cheapest good thing in this guide. It is a counter, not a restaurant: stand, eat two, pay cash, move on. Nothing dated 2026 surfaced, so treat it as likely but not proven to be trading, and keep the market itself as the fallback if the shutter is down.

tascas.title: Copper pots and small rooms
tascas.story: Faro's tascas cook the Ria Formosa in a short, fixed vocabulary: the cataplana steamed shut in its copper pot, wet razor-clam rice, clams with garlic and coriander, fish off the grill. Tasca do Ricky on Rua do Forno keeps nine tables of four at most and builds its name on the cataplana the owner recommends. A Venda on Rua do Compromisso does petiscos from scratch in a room of old furniture and odd plates, with a large vegetarian list. Adega Nova, near the station, is the big room where families celebrate over picanha cooked on a hot stone. All three are small or plain enough that hours shift, and A Venda may close for winter, so call.
tascas.where: Tasca do Ricky, Faro Centro; A Venda, Faro Centro; Adega Nova, Faro Centro

street.title: Two markets and a bifana
street.story: The street food of this coast is bought where the fish is landed. Olhão's twin red-brick halls opened in 1916 for the Algarve's largest fishing port, one for fish and one for produce, and in September 2026 were voted one of the Novas 7 Maravilhas de Portugal; Saturday adds an outdoor market on the front. Faro's own Mercado Municipal is the plainer city market, whose current building marked its 19th year in February 2026. Inside it, Snack Bar da Xica opens at seven and sells the bifana, garlic-marinated pork in a roll, for cash at the counter. All three are morning places: by early afternoon the stalls are closing.
street.where: Mercado de Olhão, Olhão; Mercado Municipal de Faro, Faro Centro; Snack Bar da Xica, Mercado Municipal de Faro
